title: Feed lines, SWR and connectors
blurb: Why coax loses more at higher frequencies, what SWR and a tuner really do, and which connector fits where.

T9B01.why: Outdoor connectors need weather protection. **Tape all of them**: PL-259, BNC and Type N.

T9B02.why: Amateur coax is almost always **50 ohms**.
T9B02.trap: 600 ohms is open-wire line, not coax.

T9B03.why: Coax is popular because it is **easy to use**: it needs few special installation precautions.
T9B03.trap: It isn't the lowest-loss or highest-power line, just the most convenient.

T9B04.why: A tuner **matches the antenna system's impedance** to the radio's output impedance.
T9B04.trap: It doesn't tune receivers or choose antennas.

T9B05.why: Coax **loss rises with frequency**. Impedance stays the same.

T9B06.why: Above 400 MHz use a **Type N**. PL-259s are for HF and VHF.
T9B06.trap: RS-213 (really RG-213) is a cable, not a connector. DB-25 is a computer connector.

T9B07.why: PL-259s are the common **HF and VHF** connector. They are threaded, not bayonet, and not watertight.

T9B08.why: Water in connectors, high SWR and extra connectors **all** add loss to coax.

T9B09.why: A **loose connection** keeps changing the impedance the line sees, so SWR bounces around.
T9B09.trap: Weather and strong signals don't make a stable antenna system flicker like this.

T9B10.why: RG-213 is thicker than RG-58, so it has **less loss at a given frequency**.
T9B10.trap: Bigger cable also handles more power, not less.

T9B11.why: **Air-insulated hardline** has the lowest loss of these feed lines.

T9B12.why: SWR is a measure of **how well a load is matched** to a transmission line. 1:1 is perfect.
